strengths: The central idea is original and potentially useful: a reward-trained MLLM adjusts textual conditioning at selected denoising timesteps while leaving the diffusion backbone frozen. This combines timestep-aware control with the portability of prompt rewriting.

The experiments cover several diffusion backbones (SD1.5, SDXL, and SDXL-Turbo), single and composite rewards, and combinations with DDPO, Diffusion-DPO, ReFL, and NPNet. The consistent ImageReward improvements support the claims of reward optimization and cross-backbone portability.

The component ablation is informative: on SD1.5, GRPO, multiple refinements, and visual feedback successively raise ImageReward from -0.2315 to 0.4344, 0.4912, and 0.6320, respectively, without a corresponding collapse in the reported auxiliary metrics.

The paper is generally well organized, provides an MDP formulation and pseudocode, and documents the policy prompts, reward prompts, model choices, LoRA settings, and core optimization hyperparameters.

The method produces meaningful improvements without needing to surpass every specialized baseline on every metric; its ability to complement several existing alignment methods is a substantive practical merit.
weaknesses: A central methodological inconsistency weakens the main claim. The formulation and Algorithm 2 describe closed-loop inference conditioned on the current denoised latent, but Section 3.3 says visual feedback is unnecessary at inference, prompts can be generated a priori, and the implementation replaces images with an image-placeholder token during sampling. Under the reported implementation, test-time control appears open-loop rather than an MDP driven by evolving latent feedback. The paper does not clearly separate training-time feedback from the inference method used for each table and figure.

The claimed mitigation of reward hacking and over-optimization is not adequately demonstrated. It is based mainly on selected qualitative examples and near-constant proxy metrics; there is no blinded human preference study, adversarial reward-hacking benchmark, reward-versus-quality curve, or comparison at matched target-reward levels. Thus the evidence supports reward improvement more strongly than robustness to reward hacking.

The quantitative evidence lacks uncertainty and essential evaluation details. The manuscript does not report evaluation sample counts for Pick-a-Pic, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Several claimed gains are extremely small, such as GenEval 0.5445 to 0.5483 and HPSv2 changes around 0.0002-0.002, so their reliability cannot be judged.

Baseline fairness is unclear. The reported RePrompt baseline is a custom ablation that explicitly removes its reasoning and multi-turn behavior, yet is labeled as the cited method. Training budgets and parameter-update budgets are not matched across prompt-policy and diffusion-tuning baselines, and the statement that baseline checkpoints were selected where evaluation rewards 'match' PromptLoop is ambiguous and potentially introduces checkpoint-selection bias.

The paper repeatedly calls the formulation 'structurally' or 'functionally equivalent' to diffusion RL, but establishes only an analogy. Discrete prompt actions passed through a frozen text encoder do not generally have the expressivity of updating the denoiser or selecting latent transitions, and no theorem or controllability analysis supports equivalence. The terminology should be narrowed to structural correspondence.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful implementation details: the number of training updates or episodes, prompt split sizes, checkpoint-selection procedure, seeds, exact default sampler configurations, and code availability are missing. The composite setup also depends on a proprietary dated GPT-5-mini reward endpoint, which may change and cannot be reproduced solely from the manuscript.

The claimed efficiency and practical plug-and-play deployment are not quantified. Five MLLM calls can add substantial latency, while closed-loop feedback may require diffusion-loop modification and memory residency. No latency, VRAM, training cost, or quality-versus-number-of-refinements tradeoff is reported against prompt-refinement baselines.

There are smaller technical and presentation issues, including inconsistent indexing in the denoised-estimate equation versus the algorithms, an apparent state/action sampling typo in the Diffusion-RL description, and the misspelling 'PrompLoops.' These are correctable, but the inference-protocol ambiguity is material rather than cosmetic.

strengths: The central idea—using an MLLM policy to revise text conditioning at selected denoising timesteps—is interesting and relevant to modular alignment of text-to-image diffusion models. It avoids modifying the diffusion backbone and can, in principle, be composed with separately aligned models.

The paper evaluates several Stable Diffusion variants and reports consistent improvements in the optimized ImageReward metric. Applying the learned policy on top of DDPO, Diffusion-DPO, ReFL, and NPNet provides useful initial evidence of composability.
The incremental ablation attributes gains to GRPO training, multiple prompt updates, and visual feedback. The qualitative prompt-evolution analysis also offers some interpretability.
The manuscript is generally organized and provides policy prompts, principal hyperparameters, algorithms, and reward definitions.
weaknesses: The paper alternates among “structural analogy,” “functional equivalence,” and “structural equivalence” to diffusion-model RL without establishing equivalence theoretically or empirically. Text-prompt actions cannot generally reproduce arbitrary parameter-level changes, and the presented MDP correspondence is primarily a relabeling of states and actions rather than evidence of equivalent control capability.

There is a consequential inconsistency in the defining mechanism. Section 3.3 says visual feedback is essential during training but unnecessary at inference, where image inputs are replaced by a placeholder and all prompts can be generated a priori. This removes trajectory-dependent feedback and therefore the claimed closed loop at deployment. Algorithm 2 nevertheless conditions on the current denoised latent, leaving it unclear which procedure produced the reported results. The denoised-estimate notation and indices in Eq. 9 and the algorithms are also inconsistent.

The evidence for mitigating reward hacking or over-optimization is inadequate. The paper provides no human evaluation, preference study, diversity analysis, or systematic adversarial assessment. The conclusion rests on selected qualitative examples and proxy metrics; several HPSv2 differences are negligible or unfavorable despite large gains on the directly optimized ImageReward.

Experimental reporting omits evaluation sample counts, random seeds, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, training duration, and matched compute budgets. Consequently, the significance and robustness of many small differences cannot be assessed. The claim of practical efficiency is also unsupported by latency, throughput, or memory measurements, despite requiring a 3B-parameter policy and multiple prompt generations.

The “RePrompt” comparison is not a faithful implementation of the cited method: it is constructed by removing components from PromptLoop and explicitly omits RePrompt's reasoning. This weakens a central comparison against prior RL prompt refinement. Checkpoint selection for other baselines is described ambiguously as choosing points where evaluation rewards “match” PromptLoop, raising additional comparability concerns.

Generalization is demonstrated only among closely related Stable Diffusion backbones, and orthogonality is mostly measured by stacking the same prompt rewriter onto existing checkpoints. There is no evaluation on a meaningfully different text-to-image architecture or prompt distribution, so claims of seamless or broad generalization are overstated.

Reproducibility remains limited: no code or trained policy release is specified, the exact Pick-a-Pic validation subset is unspecified, and the composite reward depends on a dated proprietary API model. Overall, the promising concept does not compensate for the ambiguity in the deployed method and the insufficient support for the paper's principal robustness and equivalence claims.

strengths: PromptLoop offers a useful and reasonably original formulation: a frozen diffusion model is controlled by an MLLM policy trained with GRPO to produce timestep-dependent prompts. This preserves the modularity of prompt refinement while introducing trajectory-aware training.

The empirical gains are substantial on the optimized objective. For example, ImageReward rises from 0.7244 to 1.0948 on SDXL and from 0.0816 to 0.6320 on SD1.5; composing PromptLoop with DDPO, Diffusion-DPO, ReFL, and NPNet produces further gains without retraining the policy.

The evaluation covers SD1.5, SDXL, and SDXL-Turbo, single and composite rewards, cross-backbone transfer, and several existing alignment methods. Complementary HPSv2, aesthetic, VLM, and GenEval measurements generally remain stable or improve, supporting usefulness beyond one isolated setting.

The component ablation is informative: GRPO provides the main improvement, multiple refinements add further gains, and training with visual feedback raises ImageReward from 0.4912 to 0.6320 without degrading the reported auxiliary metrics. The refinement-count analysis further supports the value of iterative prompting.

The approach is practically attractive: it does not alter diffusion weights, transfers between backbones, and can complement weight-, gradient-, and noise-based alignment. The manuscript is clear, visually polished, and provides algorithms, prompts, principal hyperparameters, and qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The strongest conceptual claim is overstated. Although the method is trained with latent feedback, the reported inference procedure replaces images with a placeholder and generates prompts in advance. Consequently, the deployed method is not actually a closed-loop policy reacting to the evolving latent trajectory. This conflicts with Algorithm 2 and weakens claims of inference-time 'structural equivalence' to diffusion RL, though it does not negate the empirical contribution.

Claims of mitigating reward hacking and over-optimization are not adequately established. They rely mainly on selected qualitative examples and the absence of degradation in proxy metrics; there is no human evaluation, systematic stress test, reward-versus-quality curve, or comparison at matched target-reward levels.

Statistical support is limited: evaluation sample counts, repeated runs, uncertainty intervals, seed controls, and significance tests are not reported. Some gains on non-target metrics are very small, and checkpoint selection is insufficiently specified—the statement that baseline checkpoints were chosen where evaluation rewards 'match those of PromptLoop' is ambiguous and may affect fairness.

Baseline coverage does not fully isolate novelty. RePrompt is a locally simplified implementation with reasoning removed, Qwen2.5-VL is left untrained, and closely related recent iterative or stage-aware methods discussed in the related work are not quantitatively compared. Compute-matched comparisons and inference latency/cost measurements are also absent despite using a 3B policy and multiple prompt updates.

There are reproducibility and technical ambiguities: the number of training prompts, optimization steps, training time, evaluation sample counts, seeds, and code-release status are missing. Equation 9 and the algorithms use inconsistent timestep/index notation for the denoised estimate, and Algorithm 2 references an initially undefined denoised state. These appear correctable but should be resolved.

strengths: The core idea is useful and reasonably original: an RL-trained MLLM changes textual conditioning at selected denoising stages while leaving the image generator frozen. This provides a modular alternative to generator fine-tuning.

The empirical scope is substantial. Results cover SD1.5, SDXL, SDXL-Turbo, FLUX.1-dev, and SD3.5-large; several reward formulations; and combinations with DDPO, ReFL, Diffusion-DPO, DanceGRPO, and NPNet.

The reported target-reward gains are often large. For example, PromptLoop raises ImageReward from 0.7244 to 1.0948 on SDXL and from 0.0816 to 0.6320 on SD1.5, while generally preserving HPSv2, aesthetic, and MLLM scores.

Ablations provide evidence that GRPO training, multiple prompt updates, and training-time visual feedback each contribute. The analysis of prompt evolution, length, and semantic retention also improves interpretability.

The frozen-generator design enables convincing zero-shot transfer and composability demonstrations, which are practically valuable even where PromptLoop does not replace the underlying alignment method.
The manuscript is generally clear and includes algorithms, prompts, major optimization hyperparameters, compute requirements, and useful qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The central closed-loop claim is internally inconsistent. The method is introduced and formalized as conditioning the policy on the current denoised latent during sampling, and Algorithm 2 requires this visual state. However, the implementation states that at inference the visual input is replaced by an image-placeholder token and that all prompts can be generated a priori. The paper does not clearly identify which inference procedure produced each main result or directly compare closed-loop inference, placeholder-based inference, and ordinary feed-forward timestep-conditioned rewriting. This obscures what mechanism actually delivers the gains.

Calling the construction “structurally equivalent” or “functionally equivalent” to diffusion-model RL is too strong. PromptLoop has a discrete language-policy action followed by a frozen diffusion transition, whereas diffusion RL directly treats image-state transitions as policy actions. The paper establishes an analogy between MDP descriptions, not equivalence in optimization, expressivity, or induced trajectory distributions.

Claims of mitigating reward hacking and improving human preference are not adequately validated. Evidence consists primarily of proxy rewards, another automated MLLM judge, and selected qualitative examples; there is no blinded human evaluation, preference rate, or systematic measurement of reward-hacking failures. The qualitative comparison with ReFL cannot by itself establish this claim.

Quantitative reliability is difficult to assess because evaluation sample counts, random seeds, repeated-run variation, confidence intervals, and significance tests are absent. Several reported improvements on non-target metrics are extremely small, such as HPSv2 changes around 0.0002–0.001, and therefore cannot be interpreted confidently.

Baseline selection and checkpointing need stronger justification. The statement that baseline checkpoints are chosen where evaluation rewards “match those of PromptLoop” is unclear and potentially introduces selection bias. Some baselines are retrained, some use released checkpoints, and RePrompt is reconstructed by removing components from the authors’ framework; this weakens the conclusiveness of direct rankings.

The visual-feedback ablation is cumulative rather than factorial, so it does not isolate interactions among visual feedback, multiple refinement, and RL. In particular, the paper lacks a controlled comparison showing whether visual feedback at inference adds value beyond a policy conditioned only on prompt history and timestep.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful implementation details: the exact training/evaluation prompt counts and splits, number of optimization updates for each setting, sampling seeds, reward normalization, failure handling for invalid JSON, and complete inference procedure are not specified. No code or trained-policy release is stated.

Runtime is measured only on one A100 setting with batch size eight and excludes a clear memory analysis. A 23% latency increase plus co-residency of a 3B MLLM is not necessarily “negligible” for single-image or commodity user-facing deployment; the paper itself acknowledges the substantial memory constraint.

strengths: The method combines RL-trained prompt rewriting with timestep conditioning and intermediate denoised-image observations, offering a modular way to optimize rewards without changing diffusion-model weights.

The empirical scope is broad: the paper studies SD1.5, SDXL, SDXL-Turbo, SD3.5, and FLUX; single and composite rewards; and composition with several existing alignment methods. The reported target-reward gains are often substantial.

Ablations suggest that GRPO training, repeated prompt updates, and training-time visual feedback each contribute. The supplementary analyses of prompt length, semantic drift, training dynamics, and prompt evolution are also useful.
The manuscript is generally readable and provides pseudocode, major training hyperparameters, qualitative results, and a runtime analysis.
weaknesses: The central framing is inconsistent with the implemented inference method. The MDP, figures, and sampling algorithm describe a closed-loop policy observing evolving latent states, but Sec. 3.3 and Appendix C.1 say inference replaces visual feedback with an image-placeholder token and can generate refinements before diffusion. The inference policy therefore cannot react to the realized denoising trajectory; operationally, it is a timestep-conditioned sequence of prompt rewrites rather than the advertised latent-feedback loop. Training with privileged visual input may still help, but it does not establish the claimed inference-time structural equivalence to diffusion RL.

The claim of mitigating reward hacking and over-optimization is inadequately supported. Evaluation relies principally on learned proxies—ImageReward, HPSv2, aesthetics, and a Qwen-based score—with no blinded human-preference study. The main evidence against reward hacking consists of a few author-selected qualitative examples. Small proxy-score changes, such as HPSv2 increasing from 0.2805 to 0.2807, cannot substantiate improved human preference without uncertainty estimates.

Quantitative reliability is difficult to assess. The Pick-a-Pic evaluation sample count and number of samples per prompt are not reported; there are no repeated seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests; and PromptLoop's total training steps and checkpoint-selection rule are omitted. The statement that DDPO/ReFL results use checkpoints whose evaluation rewards “match those of PromptLoop” is unclear and raises concern about post-hoc selection.

Several baseline comparisons are not faithful enough to support superiority claims. The RePrompt baseline is an in-house ablation that removes reasoning even though reasoning is a defining part of RePrompt. Exact prompts and decoding settings for the GPT-5 and Qwen baselines are also absent, leaving important implementation confounds.

The formal specification contains implementation-relevant gaps. Algorithms 1 and 2 may query the denoised estimate at the initial timestep before computing it; Eq. 10 and the algorithms use inconsistent denoised-estimate indices; and the manuscript does not explain how multiple autoregressive prompt actions within an episode are represented and assigned credit under token-level GRPO.

Reproducibility remains limited despite reporting hardware and some GRPO/LoRA settings. Missing details include training-set sizes and splits, optimization duration in steps, random seeds, prompt-policy decoding parameters, complete baseline prompts, exact sparse-refinement timesteps, and the local Qwen evaluator's decoding protocol. References to model defaults and standard protocols are insufficient because these choices materially affect text-to-image evaluation.

The practicality claim is overstated. Five prompt refinements raise measured latency from 15.00 to 18.43 seconds per image—a 23% increase—and peak VRAM, identified by the authors as a major bottleneck, is not measured. Runtime is evaluated only on one A100 configuration at batch size eight.

The modular idea and broad reported gains are worthwhile, but the mismatch between the claimed closed-loop contribution and actual inference, combined with insufficient support for the reward-hacking and human-preference claims and an under-controlled evaluation, makes the current evidence favor rejection.

strengths: PromptLoop offers an original and useful formulation: an MLLM policy performs timestep-aware prompt refinement, enabling reward alignment without modifying the diffusion backbone. The combination of reinforcement learning, sparse refinements, and intermediate denoised-state feedback is technically interesting and relevant to controllable image generation.

The empirical scope is strong. Results cover SD1.5, SDXL, SDXL-Turbo, several reward functions, combinations with DDPO, ReFL, DanceGRPO, Diffusion-DPO, and NPNet, plus zero-shot transfer to FLUX.1-dev and SD3.5-large. The consistent improvements support the claimed modularity and cross-backbone usefulness.

The ablations provide meaningful evidence for the main components. On SD1.5, adding GRPO, multiple refinements, and visual feedback progressively raises ImageReward from -0.2315 to 0.4344, 0.4912, and 0.6320, respectively. The refinement-step study likewise indicates that feedback is important for benefiting from additional updates.

The method improves more than its optimized metric in many settings. For example, the SDXL ImageReward policy raises ImageReward from 0.7244 to 1.0948 while also improving aesthetics and the independent MLLM score. This is encouraging evidence that the method is not merely exploiting the target reward.

The paper is generally clear and visually polished. It supplies algorithms, prompts, optimization settings, hardware and runtime information, qualitative comparisons, prompt-evolution analysis, and evidence concerning semantic drift and denoised-state interpretability.
weaknesses: The strongest claim of closed-loop latent-feedback inference is blurred by an important train-test discrepancy. Section 3.3 and Appendix C state that visual feedback can be removed at inference and replaced by an image-placeholder token, allowing all timestep prompts to be generated a priori, whereas Algorithm 2 explicitly conditions every refinement on the current denoised state. The paper should clearly distinguish the feedback-conditioned algorithm from the apparently open-loop implementation and report their performance separately. As written, the claimed deployment-time analogy to diffusion RL is not fully established.

The terms "structural equivalence" and "functional equivalence" overstate what is demonstrated. PromptLoop makes sparse, discrete text actions—two refinements during training—while diffusion RL controls continuous transitions throughout the denoising trajectory. The analogy is insightful, but no theoretical result establishes equivalence in controllability, policy class, or optimization.

Evidence for mitigating reward hacking and over-optimization is limited. The main support is a small set of qualitative comparisons and improvements on correlated automatic metrics; there is no blinded human evaluation, statistical analysis, diversity measurement, or systematic reward-versus-quality sweep. Consequently, robustness to reward hacking remains a plausible but insufficiently substantiated claim.

Important evaluation details needed to judge reliability are missing, including the number of evaluated prompts/images for the Pick-a-Pic experiments, random seeds, uncertainty or significance estimates, and run-to-run variance. The baseline checkpoint rule—selecting checkpoints where evaluation rewards "match those of PromptLoop"—is also unclear and could affect fairness. Moreover, the RePrompt baseline removes reasoning, one of that method's defining components, rather than comparing against its full reported system.

Practicality is somewhat overstated. Five refinements add 23% latency even at batch size 8 on an A100, while policy-plus-diffusion memory consumption is acknowledged but not measured. Training requires four 80GB A100 GPUs for roughly three days, and the composite setup depends on a proprietary GPT-5-mini reward. These do not invalidate the contribution, but weaken the claims of negligible overhead and straightforward reproducibility. There are also correctable indexing ambiguities in Eq. 10 and Algorithms 1–2 concerning whether the denoised estimate represents x0, x_t, or x_{t-1}.
